overview.text: Illinois is a U.S. state whose capital is Springfield and that includes Chicago; it borders Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Missouri and Wisconsin. It joined the Union on December 3, 1818, as the 21st state, and Springfield has been its capital since 1837. Its nickname, the Prairie State, reflects its once-extensive tallgrass landscape: glaciers shaped much of its northern terrain, while prairie and forest once formed contrasting regions. Most original prairie has since been converted, especially for agriculture. Illinois is also called the Land of Lincoln: Abraham Lincoln lived and worked there for decades before becoming president, and Chicago rose as a major city and economic center during the nineteenth century. The state’s mix of prairie heritage, Chicago’s urban influence and Lincoln’s history distinguishes Illinois.

key_facts.text: Illinois became the 21st state on December 3, 1818. Its capital moved from Kaskaskia to Vandalia and then to Springfield in 1837.
In 1820, Illinois had about 22 million acres of prairie and 14 million acres of forest; by 1900, most of its prairie had been converted, mainly to agriculture.
Glaciers shaped much of northern Illinois; the last major glaciation in the state was about 12,000 years ago.
Illinois’s official slogan is “Land of Lincoln,” referring to Abraham Lincoln’s years of residence and public life in the state before his presidency.
Before statehood, Illinois’s proposed northern border did not reach Lake Michigan; an amendment extended it north to make room for a future port city—Chicago—and access to lead-mining areas.
